title: B.C. family to Iran: Don't 'use us'
article: The family of Keyvan Tabesh was shocked yesterday to find themselves in the eye of a political storm.
They say they had no idea the Iranian government was going to use the death of 18-year-old Mr. Tabesh to create a diplomatic incident with Canada.
"We were surprised," said Keyvan's sister, Rita, in an interview at the door of the family's home in Burnaby. "We never talk to the government.
"The problem is between Keyvan's family and the police. It is a social problem, not a political problem."

Rita said as soon as she learned that news of her brother's death was being reported in Iran and that his name was being mentioned by Iranian government officials, she phoned her husband, who is visiting relatives in Iran, to ask him to phone TV stations there and tell them to stop broadcasting the news.
"I told him to phone the media and tell them to stop spreading news in Iran," Rita said.

Mr. Tabesh was shot July 14 by a police officer in Port Moody after an apparent road-rage incident. Police say after Mr. Tabesh had used a machete to strike another vehicle that had blocked his way, he was followed into a Port Moody cul-de-sac by an officer.

Then, according to police spokesman Const. Brian Soles, Mr. Tabesh and another passenger, Amir Aghaei, got out of their car and rushed at police. Mr. Tabesh was carrying a machete, so the officer fired five shots at him in what police say was self defence.
Mr. Tabesh was killed and Mr. Aghaei was wounded.
However, Mr. Tabesh's family disputes the story.

His mother, Forough Jabalameli, told a Toronto newspaper days after the shooting that Mr. Tabesh did not know it was a policeman who was confronting him because the officer was dressed in street clothes and driving a vehicle without any police markings.
She also said the officer shot at her son's heart without identifying himself and did not give any warning shots.
Yesterday, Rita and Mr. Tabesh's father, Nasser, didn't want to talk about what happened to Mr. Tabesh, saying only that the family plans to hire a lawyer and pursue the matter in court.

Both were clearly upset, not only by Mr. Tabesh's death, but by the Iranian government's current involvement in it, and didn't want to cause themselves or any other members of their family any more trouble.
They did, however, say Mr. Tabesh's death was not the business of the Iranian government, and they didn't want what happened to him to be used for political purposes.

An Iranian government press release announced yesterday that there is "fear and horror" among Canadian Iranians following the shooting of Mr. Tabesh. "We don't want the government to use our family," his sister said. "We just want to know why the police killed our brother."

The Tabeshes, who are landed immigrants, still have family in Iran, and want to be able to continue travel freely between both countries. Rita's elder brother, Kamyar, an engineering student at the University of British Columbia, is in Iran visiting relatives now, and didn't even know his brother had been killed, his sister said. She and her parents had decided not to tell him until he returned.
"We are not a political family," Nasser said. "We are living in Canada now and we want justice in Canada."
The Tabeshes left Iran in 2000, choosing to live in Canada for its educational opportunities, Rita said.
Mr. Tabesh was finishing his last year of high school when he was killed, Rita said. She is learning English and was a microbiologist in Iran.
According to the Globe story, her father was a decorated military surgeon in Iran, and her mother is a chemist now working for a Vancouver research firm.
"Please write about how our family is feeling," Nasser, who was unwell Thursday, said.
"We don't want to talk. We just want justice in this place -- where we are living."

Amir Aghaei was not available for comment yesterday, but his father, who declined to give his first name, said he agreed with the Tabeshes that what happened to his son was a matter for Canadian, not Iranian, authorities.
"The Iranian government are liars," Aghaei said. "This is not Iran's business. This happened in Canada, not Iran."
He said Amir has recovered from his injury, and the family plans to consult a lawyer to deal with the issue here.
